# Thoracic cavity

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Cardiothoracic surgery > Thoracic cavity*

[Original Article Link](/library/Op0IpS)

---

## Summary

The thoracic cavity is a hollow space surrounded by the <u>rib</u> cage and the <u>diaphragm</u> that contains the <u>heart</u>, <u>lungs</u>, <u>esophagus</u>, <u>thymus</u>, <u>sympathetic trunk</u>, and the great vessels. It comprises three compartments: two pleural cavities and the <u>mediastinum</u>, which is located behind the <u>sternum</u>. The <u>mediastinum</u> is divided into the superior and <u>inferior mediastinum</u>, the latter of which is further subdivided into the <u>anterior</u>, middle, and <u>posterior mediastinum</u>. Inflammation of the <u>mediastinum</u> (<u>mediastinitis</u>) can result from spreading retropharyngeal infections or contamination from perforated <u>mediastinal</u> organs. The <u>mediastinum</u> is also a potential site for <u>teratoma</u>, <u>lymphoma</u>, <u>thymoma</u>, and <u>thyroid</u> <u>neoplasm</u>. The <u>pleural cavity</u> is the potential space between the <u>parietal pleura</u> (which covers the thoracic wall and the <u>mediastinum</u>) and the <u>visceral pleura</u> (which lines the <u>lung</u>). The <u>pleura</u> secretes fluid that prevents the development of friction between the two <u>pleural membranes</u>. Excessive build-up of fluid in the <u>pleural cavity</u> results in <u>pleural effusion</u>, while the entry of air results in <u>pneumothorax</u>. The <u>diaphragm</u> is a musculotendinous structure that separates the thoracic cavity from the <u>abdominal cavity</u>. It has hiatuses for the passage of the <u>inferior vena cava</u> (<u>caval hiatus</u>), <u>esophagus</u> (<u>esophageal hiatus</u>), and the aorta (<u>aortic hiatus</u>) at the 8<sup>th</sup>, 10<sup>th</sup>, and 12<sup>th</sup> <u>thoracic vertebrae</u> respectively. The <u>diaphragm</u> is innervated by the <u>phrenic nerve</u>. <u>Phrenic nerve</u> palsy or <u>injury to the diaphragm</u> results in impaired respiration.

---

## Mediastinum

### Overview




* Definition: The <u>mediastinum</u> is the central space of the thoracic cavity located behind the <u>sternum</u> and between the two <u>lungs</u> and their respective <u>pleura</u>.  [[1]](/library/ES08Yf)

* Boundaries 

* <u>Anterior</u>: <u>sternum</u> and <u>transversus thoracis</u> muscles

* <u>Posterior</u>: <u>vertebral column</u>

* Superior: thoracic inlet

* Inferior: <u>diaphragm</u>

* <u>Lateral</u>: <u>pleura</u> of the <u>lung</u>





| <br>Compartments of the mediastinum [[1]](/library/ES08Yf) |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <br>Structure<br> |  | Boundaries | Organs | Vessels | Nerves | Causes of mediastinal masses |

| Inferior mediastinum | Anterior mediastinum | <br><br>* <u>Anterior</u>: body of the <u>sternum</u> and <u>transversus thoracis</u> muscles<br><br>* <u>Posterior</u>: <u>pericardium</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Remnants of the <u>thymus</u> (postpubertal)<br><br>* <u>Connective tissue</u> and fat<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Internal thoracic vessels<br><br>* <u>Lymphatics</u> and <u>parasternal lymph nodes</u><br><br><br> | <br>* NA<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Thymomas</u><br><br>* <u>Germ cell tumors</u> (e.g., <u>teratoma</u>)<br><br>* Retrosternal <u>thyroid</u> (substernal <u>goiter</u>) [[2]](/library/_1X5jC)<br><br>* <u>Lung cancer</u><br><br>* <u>Abscess</u><br><br>* <u>Lymphomas</u><br><br><br> |
| Middle mediastinum | <br><br>* <u>Anterior</u> and <u>posterior</u> <u>pericardium</u><br><br>* Between the two pleural cavities<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Heart</u> and <u>pericardium</u><br><br>* <u>Tracheal</u> bifurcation and the left and right main <u>bronchi</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Root of the aorta<br><br>* <u>Pulmonary trunk</u><br><br>* Pericardiacophrenic <u>artery</u><br><br>* Superior and <u>inferior vena cava</u><br><br>* Arch of the <u>azygos vein</u><br><br>* <u>Pulmonary veins</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Phrenic nerve</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Lymphomas</u><br><br>* <u>Bronchogenic cysts</u><br><br>* <u>Hiatal hernia</u><br><br>* <u>Metastases</u><br><br>* <u>Lung cancer</u><br><br>* <u>Abscess</u><br><br>* <u>Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy</u><br><br>* Vascular masses<br><br><br> |  |
| Posterior mediastinum | <br><br>* <u>Anterior</u>: fibrous <u>pericardium</u> and <u>posterior</u> sloping surface of <u>diaphragm</u><br><br>* <u>Posterior</u>: the bodies of the <u>vertebral column</u> from the lower border of the 5<sup>th</sup>–12<sup>th</sup> <u>thoracic vertebra</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Esophagus</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Thoracic portion of the aorta<br><br>* <u>Azygos vein</u>, <u>hemiazygos vein</u>, and <u>thoracic duct</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Vagus nerve</u><br><br>* <u>Sympathetic trunk</u><br><br>* <u>Splanchnic nerves</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Neurogenic tumors (most common) <br><br>* <u>Neuroendocrine tumors</u><br><br>* <u>Neurofibromas</u><br><br>* <u>Esophageal cancer</u><br><br>* <u>Multiple myeloma</u> [[3]](/library/OUbIWG)<br><br>* <u>Lymphoma</u><br><br>* <u>Lung cancer</u><br><br>* <u>Abscess</u><br><br>* <u>Aneurysm</u><br><br><br> |  |





> [!NOTE]
> The most common causes of inflammation of the <u>mediastinal</u> space (<u>mediastinitis</u>) include spreading of retropharyngeal infections into the <u>mediastinum</u>, chest trauma, and perforation of <u>mediastinal</u> organs, e.g., the <u>esophagus</u> in the course of a <u>gastroscopy</u> or due to <u>esophageal cancer</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> The <u>trachea</u> bifourcates at the level of T4.




> [!NOTE]
> The 4 T's of a <u>mediastinal mass</u>: Thymoma, Teratoma (and other <u>germ cell tumors</u>), Thyroid <u>neoplasm</u>, and Terrible <u>lymphoma</u>.

### Vasculature of the <u>mediastinum</u> [[1]](/library/ES08Yf)




#### <u>Arteries</u>




The <u>pulmonary trunk</u>, which is located in the <u>middle mediastinum</u> and conveys deoxygenated blood to the <u>lungs</u>, is discussed in “<u>Airways and lungs</u>”.




| <br>Branches of aorta in thoracic cavity<br> |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Structure | Anatomy | Location | Branches | Supplies |
| Ascending aorta | <br><br>* Originates from the aortic orifice from the <u>left ventricle</u><br><br>* Courses within the <u>pericardium</u><br><br>* Ends at the level of the <u>angle of Louis</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Middle mediastinum</u>: <u>posterior</u> to the <u>sternum</u><br><br> | <br>* At the level of the <u>aortic valve</u><br><br>* <u>Left coronary artery</u><br><br>* <u>Right coronary artery</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Heart</u><br><br> |
| Arch of the aorta | <br><br>* Continuation of the <u>ascending aorta</u><br><br>* Arches superiorly, posteriorly, and to the left before moving inferiorly<br><br>* Connected to the <u>pulmonary trunk</u> by the <u>ligamentum arteriosum</u><br><br>* Aortic isthmus: narrowing at the final section of the <u>aortic arch</u>, just <u>distal</u> to the origin of the <u>left subclavian artery</u> at the insertion site of the <u>ligamentum arteriosum</u> (former ductus arteriosum)<br><br>* Forms the aortic knob (on <u>chest x-ray</u>)<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Superior mediastinum</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Brachiocephalic trunk which then splits into <u>right subclavian artery</u> and right <u>common carotid artery</u><br><br>* Left <u>common carotid artery</u><br><br>* <u>Left subclavian artery</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Head<br><br>* Upper extremities<br><br><br> |
| <br>Thoracic aorta (Part of the descending aorta) <br> | <br><br>* Continuation of the <u>arch of the aorta</u><br><br>* Begins at the level of T4<br><br>* Leaves the thorax via the <u>aortic hiatus</u> in the <u>diaphragm</u> at the level of T12, where it becomes the <u>abdominal aorta</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Posterior mediastinum</u><br><br>* Left side of the thoracic <u>vertebral column</u> and behind the <u>esophagus</u> at its origin<br><br>* Midline of the thoracic <u>vertebral column</u> at its passage through the <u>aortic hiatus</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Bronchial arteries</u><br><br>* Mediastinal arteries<br><br>* Esophageal arteries<br><br>* Pericardial arteries<br><br>* Superior phrenic arteries<br><br>* Posterior intercostal arteries (9 pairs)<br><br>* Subcostal arteries<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Lungs</u><br><br>* <u>Mediastinum</u><br><br>* <u>Esophagus</u><br><br>* <u>Pericardium</u><br><br>* <u>Diaphragm</u><br><br>* <u>Chest wall</u><br><br><br> |

#### <u>Veins</u>




The <u>pulmonary veins</u>, which are located in the <u>middle mediastinum</u> and transfer oxygenated blood from the <u>lungs</u> to the <u>heart</u>, are discussed in “<u>Airways and lungs</u>”. <u>Cavocaval anastomoses</u> are discussed in “<u>Abdominal cavity</u>”.




| Veins in the thoracic cavity |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Structure |  | Formation | Characteristics | Tributaries |
| <br>Superior vena cava (<u>SVC</u>) |  | <br>* Formed by the junction between the left and right <u>brachiocephalic veins</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Drains blood from structures above the <u>diaphragm</u> → <u>right atrium</u> of the <u>heart</u><br><br>* The <u>SVC</u> can be divided into two main parts:<br><br>* The upper half is located in the <u>superior mediastinum</u><br><br>* The lower half is located in the <u>middle mediastinum</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Mediastinal</u> <u>veins</u><br><br>* Esophageal <u>veins</u><br><br>* <u>Pericardial</u> <u>veins</u><br><br><br> |
| Brachiocephalic veins |  | <br>* Formed by the <u>convergence</u> of the jugular <u>vein</u> and the <u>subclavian vein</u> at the <u>venous angle</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Receive blood from the <u>chest wall</u>, neck, <u>esophagus</u>, <u>lungs</u>, and <u>pericardium</u><br><br>* The right <u>brachiocephalic vein</u> is short and is more vertically oriented, while the left <u>brachiocephalic vein</u> is long and has more horizontal orientation.<br><br>* The right and left <u>vein</u> merge to form the <u>superior vena cava</u>.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Vertebral</u> <u>veins</u><br><br>* <u>Internal thoracic veins</u><br><br>* Inferior <u>thyroid</u> <u>veins</u><br><br><br> |
| Azygos venous system | Azygos vein | <br>* Formed by the right subcostal and <u>ascending lumbar veins</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Courses along the right side of the thoracic <u>vertebral column</u><br><br>* Unpaired <u>vein</u> that drains into <u>superior vena cava</u><br><br>* Enters the thorax via the <u>aortic hiatus</u> of the <u>diaphragm</u><br><br>* Connected to the <u>inferior vena cava</u> (<u>IVC</u>) inferiorly<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Hemiazygos vein</u><br><br>* <u>Bronchial veins</u><br><br>* <u>Pericardial</u> <u>veins</u><br><br>* Esophageal <u>veins</u><br><br>* Right posterior intercostal veins (run along the undersurface of the corresponding <u>rib</u>)<br><br><br> |
| Hemiazygos vein | <br>* Formed by the ascending lumbar and left subcostal <u>veins</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Courses along the left side of the <u>vertebral column</u> and passes behind the aorta<br><br>* Unpaired <u>vein</u> that drains into the <u>azygos vein</u><br><br>* Enters the thorax via <u>aortic hiatus</u> or the left crus of the <u>diaphragm</u><br><br>* Connected to the left <u>renal vein</u> inferiorly<br><br><br> | <br><br>* 9th–11th left <u>posterior intercostal veins</u><br><br>* Left superior phrenic <u>vein</u><br><br>* <u>Accessory hemiazygos vein</u><br><br><br> |  |
| Accessory hemiazygos vein | <br>* Formed by the 4<sup>th</sup> to 8<sup>th</sup> left <u>posterior intercostal veins</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Unpaired <u>vein</u> that usually drains into the <u>azygos vein</u> at the level T8<br><br>* Located on the left side of the <u>vertebral column</u><br><br><br> | <br>* 4th–8th left <u>posterior intercostal veins</u><br><br> |  |





> [!NOTE]
> The <u>azygos vein</u> connects the inferior and <u>superior vena cava</u> and can be an <u>alternative pathway</u> for deoxygenated blood to return to the <u>right atrium</u> if the <u>SVC</u> or the <u>IVC</u> are obstructed.

## Pleura

### Overview [[1]](/library/ES08Yf)




Definition: <u>Pleura</u> is a thin double layer of tissue that surrounds the <u>lungs</u> and the thoracic wall and divided into a <u>visceral</u> and parietal layer.




| Layers of pleura |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Structure | Parietal pleura | Visceral pleura |
| Location | <br><br>* Lines the inner surface of the thoracic wall and the <u>mediastinum</u><br><br>* Divided into the following parts<br><br>* Cervical (projects above the first <u>cervical rib</u> into the neck)<br><br>* <u>Mediastinal</u><br><br>* Costal<br><br>* Diaphragmatic<br><br><br> | <br>* Lines the outer surface of the <u>lungs</u> and follows the contour of the <u>lungs</u>, including the fissures<br><br> |
| Blood supply | <br><br>* <u>Internal thoracic artery</u><br><br>* <u>Posterior</u> and superior <u>intercostal arteries</u><br><br>* Superior phrenic <u>artery</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Bronchial arteries</u><br><br> |
| Innervation | <br><br>* Costal part: <u>intercostal nerve</u> (very sensitive to <u>pain</u>)<br><br>* Diaphragmatic part: <u>phrenic nerve</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Pulmonary plexus</u> derived from the <u>sympathetic trunk</u> and <u>vagus nerve</u> (not sensitive to <u>pain</u>, temperature, or touch)<br><br> |
| Clinical significance | <br>* <u>Rib fractures</u>, <u>pleuritis</u>, and pleural masses (e.g., mesotheliomas) cause sharp <u>chest pain</u> that is worse with inhalation (pleuritic).<br><br> | <br>* Intrapulmonary pathologies (e.g., <u>lung cancer</u>) do not cause <u>pain</u> and remain unnoticed for a long time.<br><br> |





### Pleural cavity [[1]](/library/ES08Yf)




* Location: potential space between the parietal and <u>visceral pleura</u> of the <u>lungs</u>

* Content: pleural fluid (secreted by serous membranes in the <u>pleura</u>)

* Lubricates and prevents friction between the parietal and <u>visceral pleura</u>

* Produces a surface tension that draws the two <u>pleura</u> layers together, ensuring simultaneous extension of the thorax and <u>lungs</u> during respiration

* Recesses

* Costomediastinal recess: region where the <u>mediastinal</u> and costal <u>pleura</u> meet

* Costodiaphragmatic recess: region where the costal and diaphragmatic <u>pleura</u> meet 

* Provides potential space for the <u>lungs</u> to expand during inspiration and movement of the <u>diaphragm</u>

* Potential space for air, blood, and/or fluid accumulation (e.g., <u>pleural effusion</u>, <u>pneumothorax</u>, <u>hemothorax</u>)





> [!NOTE]
> If air enters the <u>pleural cavity</u>, the surface tension between the parietal and <u>visceral pleura</u> of the <u>lungs</u> is lost, letting the <u>lungs</u> collapse due to their natural tendency to collapse or recoil (<u>pneumothorax</u>).




> [!NOTE]
> Excessive fluid in the <u>pleural cavity</u> results in <u>pleural effusion</u>.

## Diaphragm

### Overview [[1]](/library/ES08Yf)




* Structure 

* C-shaped musculotendinous structure that separates the thoracic cavity from the <u>abdominal cavity</u>

* Forms a dome between the two cavities, with the superior surface making the floor of the thoracic cavity, and the inferior surface making the roof of the <u>abdominal cavity</u>

* Anatomically, the <u>diaphragm</u> is divided into a right and left hemidiaphragm; however, the <u>diaphragm</u> is a continuous structure.

* The right hemidiaphragm is higher than the left due to the presence of the <u>liver</u>.

* Function

* Separates the thoracic cavity from the <u>abdominal cavity</u>

* Key muscle of inspiration





### Parts of the <u>diaphragm</u> [[1]](/library/ES08Yf)




#### Crura of the diaphragm




* Definition: musculotendinous bundles that attach to the <u>anterior</u> surface of the <u>vertebral column</u>, <u>intervertebral disc</u>, and the <u>anterior longitudinal ligament</u>

* Origin: <u>lumbar vertebrae</u> (L1, L2, L3) and <u>medial</u> and <u>lateral</u> arcuate <u>ligaments</u> (on the sides)

* Insertion: <u>central tendon</u>

* Structure

* Right crus: longer

* Left crus: shorter

* The right and left crura join together via the <u>median arcuate ligament</u>.

* The <u>diaphragm</u> also attaches to the <u>medial</u> and <u>lateral</u> arcuate <u>ligaments</u>





#### Costal diaphragm




* Origin: lower six <u>ribs</u> and <u>xiphoid process</u>

* Insertion: <u>central tendon</u>





#### Central tendon of the diaphragm



* Location: point of <u>convergence</u> of the peripherally located muscles that make up the <u>diaphragm</u>




#### Structures passing through the diaphragm




| <u>Openings of the diaphragm</u> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Opening | Level | Structure |
| Caval hiatus | <br>* T8<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>IVC</u><br><br>* Right <u>phrenic nerve</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Esophageal hiatus <br> | <br>* T10<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Esophagus</u><br><br>* <u>Vagus nerve</u> (<u>anterior</u> and <u>posterior</u> trunk)<br><br><br> |
| <br>Aortic hiatus <br> | <br>* T12<br><br> | <br><br>* Aorta<br><br>* <u>Thoracic duct</u><br><br>* <u>Azygos vein</u><br><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> I ate (read 8) ten Eggs At twelve: Inferior vena cava passes the <u>diaphragm</u> at T8, the Esophagus at T10, and the Aorta at T12.




> [!NOTE]
> The <u>vagus nerve</u> (<u>CN X</u>) passes through the <u>diaphragm</u> at T10.




> [!NOTE]
> The protrusion of an abdominal structure/organ into the thorax through a lax diaphragmatic <u>esophageal hiatus</u> is referred to as a <u>hiatal hernia</u>.




### Vasculature and innervation of the diaphragm




|  | Anatomy |
| --- | --- |
| Arterial supply | <br><br>* Superior and <u>inferior phrenic arteries</u> (<u>branches of the thoracic aorta</u>)<br><br>* Branches of the <u>internal thoracic artery</u><br><br>* Musculophrenic <u>arteries</u><br><br>* Pericardiacophrenic <u>artery</u><br><br><br> |
| Venous drainage | <br>* Superior and <u>inferior phrenic veins</u><br><br> |
| Innervation | <br><br>* <u>Phrenic nerve</u> (C3–C5)<br><br>* Inferior <u>intercostal nerves</u> and <u>subcostal nerves</u> (sensory innervation to peripheral parts of the <u>diaphragm</u>)<br><br>* <u>Pain</u> is referred to the <u>trapezius</u> ridge (C3, C4) or the shoulder (C5) with <u>diaphragm</u> irritation of the respective side (e.g., <u>pneumoperitoneum</u>, <u>hematoperitoneum</u>, <u>peritonitis</u>, <u>peritoneal</u> <u>abscess</u>, <u>cholecystitis</u>, <u>splenic rupture</u>).<br><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> C3, C4, C5 keeps the <u>diaphragm</u> alive.




> [!NOTE]
> <u>Injuries to the diaphragm</u> or <u>phrenic nerve</u> palsies result in respiratory abnormalities because the <u>diaphragm</u> is the primary muscle of respiration.

## Clinical significance

### <u>Mediastinum</u>




#### Brachiocephalic vein obstruction [[4]](/library/GkYB66)[[5]](/library/tkYXp6)




* Etiology: <u>thrombosis</u> (e.g., due to <u>central vein</u> catheter), stenosis, external compression, or vascular <u>tumor</u> invasion (e.g., due to apical <u>lung tumor</u>, <u>lymphoma</u>, <u>thymoma</u>, <u>seminoma</u>)

* Clinical features

* Unilateral upper extremity swelling, <u>pain</u>, and <u>weakness</u>

* Unilateral facial and neck swelling, venous dilatation

* Treatment

* <u>Balloon angioplasty</u> with or without <u>stenting</u>

* Surgical bypass in resistant cases





#### Others




* <u>Mediastinitis</u>

* <u>Pneumomediastinum</u>

* Retrosternal <u>thyroid</u> (substernal <u>goiter</u>)

* <u>Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy</u>

* <u>Mediastinal</u> tumors

* <u>Thymoma</u> (most common primary <u>anterior</u> <u>mediastinal</u> <u>tumor</u>)

* <u>Lymphomas</u> (<u>Hodgkin lymphoma</u>, <u>non-Hodgkin lymphoma</u>)

* <u>Pheochromocytoma</u>

* <u>Extragonadal germ cell tumors</u> (e.g., <u>teratoma</u>)

* <u>Mediastinal</u> vessels

* <u>Aortic dissection</u>

* <u>Aortic rupture</u>

* <u>Aortitis</u>

* <u>Aortic aneurysm</u>

* <u>Aortic coarctation</u>

* <u>Superior vena cava syndrome</u>

* <u>Chylothorax</u>
